newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-WOODS MAINTAINS ONE-SHOT LEAD AT QUAD CITY CLASSIC.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-WOODS MAINTAINS ONE-SHOT LEAD AT QUAD CITY CLASSIC.

text.p: Twenty-year-old Tiger Woods, stepping up to a difficult challenge, fired a 67 Saturday to retain a one-shot lead after three rounds of the $1.2 million Quad City Classic at the Oakwood Country Club.
Woods, playing in only his third tournament since turning professional, stood at 10-under-par 200, one stroke better than Ed Fiori, who also carded a 67.
Woods, the three-time U.S. Amateur champion, needs a win or appproximately $110,000 in prize money in the remaining PGA events to receive a Tour exemption for next year.
He took a bold step toward his goal on Saturday.
"Today was a big jump for me," Woods said. "It's the first time I had a lead in a tour event, slept with it and kept it. That's a huge leap for me."
U.S. Open champion Steve Jones and Jay Delsing both fired 67s and were tied for third at seven-under 203. Hugh Royer III shot a 65 and for sole possession of fifth place at 204.

Woods sank a 12-foot birdie putt on the first hole before bogeying the second and fourth holes. After Woods parred the next two holes, he birdied four of the next five before parring out the final seven holes.
"I started off well, had a little trouble and then got my round squared up," said Woods. "I got frustrated but I kept my train of thought and they (putts) started to fall."

Woods earned $2,544 for a tie for 60th at the Greater Milwaukee Open and $37,500 for a tied for 11th at last week's Canadian Open. He is 204th on the money list and only the top 125 gain exempt status for 1997.
Fiori, seeking his first title in 14 years, had a bogey-free round, with birdies on the first, eighth and 10th holes.
"I played well today," said Fiori, who had back surgery four months ago. "I was a little nervous but got calm with a birdie on the first hole.
"I'd love to beat him (Woods). He's the real deal. I'd love to prevent him from winning his first title," said Fiori, who made it clear it was nothing personal.
"He's a nice kid and a good player."
First prize in the event, whose field is weakened with many top players participating in the Presidents Cup, is $180,000.
